title: Model Question Paper 1
meta: Time: 3 hours · Maximum marks: 100 · Modelled on the April 2026 NIOS paper (new syllabus)
instructions: The question paper consists of 27 questions. All questions are compulsory; where there is an OR, answer one.
Questions 1–13 are objective (MCQ, True/False, match, fill in the blanks, one word) of 1 mark per part.
Questions 14–19 carry 2 marks (30–40 words). Question 21 has five parts of 2 marks. Questions 20 and 27 carry 3 marks, 22 and 24–26 carry 4 marks, and 23 carries 6 marks (150–200 words).
Questions from previous NIOS papers show the exam they appeared in.

sections.passage: Good concentration is important to improve the memory. Learning and memorising by understanding and recalling what one has learnt is helpful. Organising and framing a logical relationship is important. Mastery not just of the content of the subject, but also the process of answering is equally important. Anxiety and fear hamper recall and result in a mental block during examination. Watching television for a long time could lower academic performance. It 'steals' away the reading time. Time management is about self-discipline. Time must be managed between filled and unfilled time. Filled time is the time spent sleeping, bathing, eating, dressing and attending school. A student has 10 hours of unfilled time. How best is the student going to utilise this? Make a timetable for the 10 hours. Seven to eight hours of sleep is necessary for optimal physical rest and brain functioning. A positive thought is the seed of a positive result. Always feel positive. This will help to lessen stress. If a student has symptoms of anxiety or depression, seek medical help immediately.

What example does the passage give to illustrate the strain caused by unpaid loans?
options: A borrower refusing to take vacations
A friend waiting for repayment while the borrower enjoys a luxury vacation
A lender asking for money back immediately
A family member refusing to lend money

questions.q: What is the overall tone of the passage?
The word 'rift' in the passage most nearly means —

sections.passage:
Money is often considered one of the most important aspects of our lives. Yet, wealth can also become a source of conflict, straining our connections, relationships, and friendships. In many cases, it is the root cause of bonds breaking apart.

People frequently turn to friends or family for financial support. However, when borrowed money is not repaid on time, rifts begin to appear. Lending money is usually an act of trust and compassion, but it can easily be taken for granted. Emotional ties often prevent both parties from setting clear repayment schedules. The lender may feel embarrassed to ask for the money back, while the borrower may start avoiding the person altogether.

Consider the example of a friend waiting for repayment while you are away on a luxury vacation. Such situations not only put your friendship at risk but also create resentment. Borrowing money from loved ones alters the balance of power in relationships, often leaving one party feeling exploited.

Ultimately, the easiest way to damage a relationship is to borrow or lend money. To preserve trust and harmony, it is wiser to avoid mixing finances with personal bonds.

questions.q: Nano-ceramic coatings on cars help prevent damage from UV rays and bird droppings.
Without nanotechnology, car paint remains unaffected by sunlight and contaminants.
Nanomaterials like carbon nanotubes make sports equipment lighter and more durable.
Tennis balls with nano-clays lose bounce quickly and cannot last through long matches.
Nanotechnology has influenced the design of golf clubs, skateboards, racquets and bikes.

sections.passage:
Vehicles and the sports industry benefit from nanotechnology. What if your poor car is parked in the sun the whole day? It may not faint; but its paint fades, blisters develop and eventually flakes off, not to mention the dust and bird droppings. Luckily, your car manufacturer has got everything 'covered'. Vehicles these days have nano-ceramic coatings that mix with sealants. These nano-coatings protect the vehicles from UV light, contaminants and the corrosive uric acid in bird droppings.

The sports industry has developed carbon nanotubes or silica nanoparticles, which when applied to sports equipment, enhance their performance. These nanomaterials render the equipment light-weight, reduce its wear and tear, and increase its strength and durability. Tennis balls with nano-clays applied on the interiors have optimal ball bounce, zero leakage and high durability to last through lengthy matches. Coming up with improved light-weight golf clubs, skateboards, tennis racquets and sports bikes, nanotechnology has charmed even celebrity sportspersons into becoming its fans.

questions.q: Why was John considered a proud captain in the Marine Police Force?
questions.answer: He had served the department responsibly for eight years, loved the sea and had spent years catching criminals at sea, fighting the wrongs of society.

questions.q: How did John spend his leisure time with friends while off duty?

questions.q: Why did David worry about catching the polluting ship named Molly?
questions.answer: Molly was much faster than their small boat, so David feared they would never be able to catch it.

questions.q: How did John's friends show their support for protecting the ocean?
questions.answer: They stood beside him at the shore, called polluting the sea a crime against nature and said they supported the Marine Police Force in stopping the polluters.

sections.passage:
John was the captain of a ship and a proud member of the Marine Police Force. He had served the department with complete responsibility for eight years. He loved sailing; the smell of the sea and the freshness of the wind made him feel calm and rejuvenated. He had spent a part of his life catching criminals at sea, and pursuing them gave him strength to fight the wrongs of society.

One day, off duty, John was sailing with his friends James, Sam and David. They spent time fishing and laughing together. "John, you finally get a break from chasing criminals!" said James. "Yes, but the sea always keeps me alert," John smiled.

On their way back, in the middle of the ocean, they saw a ship releasing a huge amount of oil into the water. "They're poisoning the sea!" cried Sam. John shouted across the waves, "Stop! What you're doing is illegal!" Instead of stopping, the ship sped away. "Their ship is too fast. We'll never catch them in this boat," said David, worried. "Then we'll report them. No one escapes the Marine Police Force," said John.

At the shore John radioed the base: a ship named Molly had been releasing oil into the sea. His friends stood beside him. "Polluting the sea is a crime against nature. We support the Marine Police Force," said Sam. "Count us in, John. The ocean deserves protection," added David. The whole force searched for Molly, and after hours of pursuit it was seized. Smuggled goods were found on board: the men were polluters and smugglers too. The culprits were arrested, and John was honoured at the headquarters for his vigilance and leadership. He called it an unforgettable experience.

questions.q: Write a paragraph (150–200 words) discussing the distraction caused by the excessive use of mobile phones by children.
questions.answer:
Mobile Phones and Children
Mobile phones have become constant companions of children today. They are useful for online classes, information and keeping in touch, but their excessive use has become a serious distraction. Many children spend hours on games, short videos and social media, and lose track of time. Studies suffer because attention keeps shifting to notifications, and homework is left half done. Late-night scrolling cuts into sleep, so children feel tired and irritable in class. Physical play and outdoor games are replaced by screens, leading to poor fitness, eye strain and bad posture. Children also talk less with their families and friends face to face, and some are exposed to unsuitable content or cyberbullying. Parents and teachers must work together: phones should be kept away during study and meal times, screen time should be limited, and children should be encouraged to take up sports, reading and hobbies. Used wisely, the mobile phone can be a good servant; used without control, it becomes a bad master.

or.q: (b) Read passage (b) above and write a summary of it in your own words.
or.answer: Built heritage — historic buildings, monuments, sites, artefacts and archives — is one of humanity's greatest treasures. It records the creativity, skill and values of past societies. Museums and archives preserve objects and documents that help us study history, art and technology and protect our cultural identity, while monuments are symbols of shared memory and pride that attract tourists and promote cultural exchange. They also give students and researchers a direct link with the past. Today rapid urbanisation, pollution and neglect threaten this heritage, but techniques such as 3D scanning, digital archiving and careful restoration help to preserve it. Protecting built heritage lets future generations learn from their ancestors and reminds us of our shared humanity.

sections.passage:
(a) You start your breakfast. Assume you are eating bread today. Ask what is the bread made of? And how? You pretty soon find out that bread is made of wheat. You ask again: "But how do we grow wheat?" Then you have to ask a farmer. He tells you how he grows wheat. But you are not satisfied. You want to know why a seed (the grain) sprouts into a small plant. This plant then grows and produces more grains on its body like a flower. We then dry this flower and thrash it to give us more grains of wheat. From one grain of wheat we got many more grains. Why? How? We get the answers to these detailed questions from the science of agriculture. In the next chapter, we will learn more about India's, agriculture.

We need water to drink, and it can come from a tank, well, river, or tap. But not all sources are safe. Water from a dirty tank may upset our stomach, so science helps us understand why. In laboratories, samples are analysed using instruments like microscopes, which reveal tiny organisms invisible to the naked eye. These organisms can harm our bodies if consumed. Science shows that boiling water kills them, making it safe to drink. Other impurities may also exist, requiring different scientific methods to remove. Thus, science ensures safe drinking water. Not everyone boils water, and some sources may naturally be pure, while some people's stomachs resist impurities. Even this variation is explained by science. What matters is the clear lesson: clean water is essential, and science provides the knowledge and methods to secure it. Through these insights, science safeguards one of our most basic human needs.

Science continues to shape modern life in ways that touch nearly every aspect of human existence. Beyond ensuring safe drinking water, it has revolutionized sanitation and hygiene. Water purification systems, chlorination, and filtration plants now provide clean water to millions, reducing the spread of diseases. In cities, sewage treatment plants prevent contamination of rivers and groundwater, safeguarding public health. From the smallest household need to global challenges, science has become the invisible force that sustains modern living, making life healthier, safer, and more convenient for mankind.

So, Science has transformed modern life in countless ways, making everyday living more efficient, healthier, and more connected. In transportation, high- speed trains, airplanes, and electric vehicles have reduced distances and made travel faster and more sustainable. In communication, mobile phones and the internet allow instant sharing of information, bridging cultures and communities across the globe. In healthcare, advanced diagnostic tools, vaccines, and surgical techniques have saved millions of lives and improved longevity. Agriculture has also benefited through mechanization, genetically improved crops, and irrigation systems that ensure food security for growing populations. Even in homes, science has simplified life with appliances, renewable energy solutions, and smart technologies that enhance comfort and safety. Entertainment, too, has been revolutionized with digital platforms, virtual reality, and streaming services that bring creativity to our fingertips. From education to industry, science continues to empower mankind, offering opportunities for progress and shaping a future that is more sustainable, inclusive, and innovative.

OR

(b) Built heritage is one of the most valuable treasures of human civilization, reflecting the creativity, skill, and achievements of societies across centuries. It includes historic buildings, monuments, sites, artefacts, and archives that embody cultural, artistic, architectural, and technological milestones. These structures and objects are not merely remnants of the past; they are living testimonies of human ingenuity and resilience. From ancient temples and forts to colonial-era buildings and modern museums, each piece of built heritage tells a story of the people who created it, their values, and their way of life.

Museums and archives preserve artefacts and documents that provide insights into history, traditions, and innovations. They allow us to study the evolution of art, science, and technology while safeguarding cultural identity. Monuments and historic sites, on the other hand, serve as symbols of collective memory and pride. They attract visitors from around the world, fostering tourism and intercultural exchange. Built heritage also plays a vital role in education, offering students and researchers tangible connections to the past.

In modern times, conservation of built heritage has become essential. Rapid urbanization, pollution, and neglect threaten these treasures. Science and technology now aid in preservation through advanced techniques like 3D scanning, digital archiving, and sustainable restoration methods. Protecting built heritage ensures that future generations can learn from and appreciate the achievements of their ancestors. Ultimately, these structures and artefacts remind us of our shared humanity, bridging the past with the present and inspiring us to build a future rooted in respect for culture and history.
